title: SHOULD WE BAPTIZE BABIES… OR ARE WE PUTTING WATER BEFORE FAITH?
paragraphs: SHOULD WE BAPTIZE BABIES… OR ARE WE PUTTING WATER BEFORE FAITH?
One of Christianity’s Most Emotional Disagreements—And the Uncomfortable Question Every Parent, Pastor, and Believer Must Face About Baptism, Salvation, and What Jesus Actually Commanded.
A mother stands at the front of a church, holding her newborn baby.
The child is barely old enough to recognize her voice. Tiny fingers curl around hers. The congregation watches quietly as a minister approaches with water.
A prayer is spoken.
Water touches the baby's forehead.
And somewhere in that sanctuary, a grandmother begins to cry.
Not because she is sad.
Because she believes something holy has just happened.
She believes her grandchild has been welcomed into God's covenant family.
She believes this moment matters for eternity.
Now travel to another church, perhaps just a few streets away.
A seventeen-year-old boy stands trembling in a baptismal pool.
His past is complicated.
He has lied to his parents. Hidden addictions. Questioned whether God was real. Spent nights feeling so ashamed of himself that he wondered whether Jesus could possibly want someone like him.
But something changed.
He heard the Gospel.
He repented.
He believed.
And now, with tears running down his face, he declares that Jesus Christ is his Lord.
The pastor lowers him beneath the water.
When he rises, the congregation erupts in praise.
Two churches.
Two baptisms.
Two families convinced they are honoring Jesus.
But here is the question that can make even devoted Christians uncomfortable:
Did Jesus command us to baptize people before they believe, or to baptize those who have personally responded to the Gospel?
And if Christians have disagreed about this for centuries, how do we know which understanding is faithful to Scripture?
Before you answer, consider something.
The mother holding that baby may love Jesus with all her heart.
The teenager entering that baptismal pool may genuinely have been transformed by grace.
And neither family's sincerity, by itself, settles the biblical question.
Because love does not eliminate our responsibility to examine Scripture.
Tradition does not become truth merely because it is old.
And something does not become false simply because it is practiced by a church different from ours.
We must go deeper.
Not to win an argument.
Not to humiliate another denomination.
Not to turn the sacred name of Jesus into ammunition for religious superiority.
But because baptism matters.
The Gospel matters.
And the difference between trusting Christ and trusting a religious ceremony matters more than many people realize.
Perhaps you were baptized as a baby.
Perhaps you were baptized as an adult.
Perhaps you have never been baptized at all.
Or perhaps you are a parent who genuinely wants to do what is right before God, but you are afraid of making the wrong decision for your child.
Stay with this question.
Because somewhere beneath the centuries of theological debate lies something far more personal:
When God looks at you, is He looking for water on your skin—or faith in His Son?
The answer begins with Jesus.
After His resurrection, Christ gave His disciples a command that would carry the Gospel across generations and nations.
Matthew 28:19–20 records His commission to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything He commanded.
The original Greek begins with a crucial expression:
μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη
mathēteusate panta ta ethnē
“Make disciples of all the nations.”
The central imperative is mathēteusate—make disciples.
The passage then uses the participles baptizontes and didaskontes, describing baptizing and teaching as activities involved in making disciples.
That matters.
Jesus did not present baptism as an isolated religious performance disconnected from discipleship.
He placed baptism inside the mission of bringing people under His lordship.
But we must be careful.

Matthew 28 does not explicitly state the minimum age of a baptismal candidate. Christians who baptize infants understand the command as including the children of believers within the covenant community, with lifelong instruction following baptism.
Christians who practice believer's baptism understand the command as directing the church to baptize people who have become disciples through faith.
Both appeal to the passage.
The disagreement is not whether Jesus commanded baptism.
He did.
The disagreement concerns who should receive it, what it signifies, and how it relates to faith.
And that is why we cannot stop at one verse.
We must follow the testimony of Scripture.
Travel with me to Jerusalem.
It is Pentecost.
The apostle Peter is preaching.
The crowd hears that the Jesus they crucified has been raised from the dead and exalted as Lord and Messiah.
Suddenly, the message becomes personal.
These are not spectators listening to an interesting religious lecture.
They are people confronted by the reality of their sin.
Acts 2:37 says they were pierced to the heart.
Imagine the silence.
Imagine realizing that the One you rejected was the very Savior God had sent.
They ask:
“What shall we do?”
Peter answers in Acts 2:38:
Μετανοήσατε ... καὶ βαπτισθήτω ἕκαστος ὑμῶν
Metanoēsate ... kai baptisthētō hekastos hymōn
“Repent ... and let each of you be baptized.”
The first word, metanoēsate, is a command to repent.
The verb baptisthētō calls for baptism.
Peter joins repentance and baptism in his response to people who have heard the Gospel.
Then Acts 2:41 describes those who received his message being baptized.
Read that again.
They heard.
They received the message.
They were baptized.
For advocates of believer's baptism, this is a powerful example of the New Testament pattern.
The Gospel is proclaimed.
People respond.
Baptism follows.
But Peter also says something that Christians must not overlook.
In Acts 2:39, he declares that the promise is for his hearers, their children, and those far away—everyone whom the Lord calls.
Those who baptize infants see significant covenantal implications in that mention of children.

Those who advocate believer's baptism emphasize the concluding qualification: the promise extends to those whom God calls, and the immediate narrative describes people receiving the apostolic message.
The verse deserves more than a slogan.
It demands careful interpretation.
Now consider the Ethiopian official in Acts 8.
He is traveling along a desert road, reading from the prophet Isaiah.
He does not understand whom the prophet is describing.
God sends Philip to him.
Philip begins with the Scripture and announces the good news about Jesus.
Then they come upon water.
The Ethiopian asks what prevents him from being baptized.
And the narrative tells us that Philip baptizes him.
The central movement is unmistakable.
Scripture is explained.
Christ is proclaimed.
Baptism follows.
Some Bible translations include an additional statement in Acts 8:37 in which Philip requires belief with all the heart and the Ethiopian confesses Jesus as the Son of God.
But there is an important textual detail.
Acts 8:37 is absent from several of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and is generally treated by modern textual scholars as a later addition.
That means we should not build an entire doctrine on that disputed verse as though its textual status were beyond question.
The surrounding account, however, still describes an adult hearing the Gospel and requesting baptism.
And the wider book of Acts repeatedly connects baptism with the spread of the Gospel.
In Acts 10, Cornelius and those gathered with him hear Peter preach. The Holy Spirit comes upon the hearers, and Peter orders them to be baptized.
In Acts 16, the Philippian jailer hears the message of the Lord and is baptized with his household.
In Acts 18:8, many Corinthians hear, believe, and are baptized.
These accounts provide substantial support for the practice of baptizing professing believers.
But then comes the question that has divided Christians for generations.
What about the households?
The New Testament records household baptisms, including Lydia's household in Acts 16, the jailer's household in the same chapter, and the household of Stephanas in 1 Corinthians 1.
Those who support infant baptism argue that the household language fits the ancient biblical pattern in which God's covenant dealings extend to families.
Those who support believer's baptism respond that none of these accounts explicitly identifies an infant being baptized.
And they are correct about that specific observation.
The New Testament does not give us an unambiguous narrative saying, “An infant was baptized.”
But the opposite claim also requires caution.
The household accounts do not always specify the age and spiritual response of every person involved.
The jailer's household is associated with hearing the word of the Lord and rejoicing over faith in God, although interpreters debate precisely how the language applies to each household member.
Lydia's household is baptized, but the narrative does not tell us the ages of its members.
Therefore, the household passages are important evidence in the debate, but they do not settle it by themselves.
We cannot honestly make the Bible say more than it says.
And perhaps that is where some of our arguments have gone wrong.
We become so determined to defend our position that we stop distinguishing between what Scripture explicitly teaches and what our theological conclusions infer.
But God does not need us to exaggerate His Word to defend it.
Now we must enter the deepest part of the discussion.
The covenant.
Because Christians who baptize infants are not necessarily claiming that babies have personally repented or consciously professed faith.
Many are making a different argument altogether.
They are asking whether the children of believers should receive the covenant sign because they belong to a household set apart within God's visible covenant community.
In Genesis 17, God commands Abraham to circumcise the males of his household, including infant sons on the eighth day.
The Hebrew word for covenant is:
בְּרִית
berit — “covenant.”
A covenant is not merely a casual promise.
It establishes a binding relationship, with obligations and promises defined by God.
Under the Abrahamic covenant, infant boys received circumcision before they could personally understand or articulate faith.
For many Presbyterian and Reformed Christians who practice infant baptism, this is a foundational part of the argument.
They see baptism as the new-covenant sign that corresponds to circumcision, with Colossians 2:11–12 forming part of their biblical reasoning.
They also appeal to the continuity of God's covenant purposes across generations.

Other traditions that baptize infants, including Catholic, Orthodox, and some Lutheran and Anglican churches, emphasize different combinations of covenant theology, sacramental grace, regeneration, and the faith of the Church.
These traditions should not be treated as though they all teach precisely the same theology of baptism.
Some regard baptism as a means through which God ordinarily gives regenerating grace.
Others emphasize incorporation into the visible covenant community while distinguishing that outward membership from inward salvation.
But here is the question believer's-baptism advocates raise.
Does the New Testament actually command the church to apply baptism to infants because circumcision was applied to infants?
Colossians 2:11–12 connects circumcision made without hands, burial with Christ in baptism, and resurrection with Him through faith in the working of God.
Believer's-baptism advocates emphasize that Paul speaks of spiritual circumcision and faith, not an explicit command to baptize infants.
Infant-baptism advocates see continuity between covenant signs and God's covenant dealings with families.
This is a genuine interpretive disagreement.
It cannot be resolved responsibly by pretending that one side has no biblical argument.
But neither should we pretend that the New Testament explicitly commands infant baptism.
It does not.
And that observation carries weight.
Especially when the clearest narrative examples of baptism repeatedly involve people who hear and respond to the Gospel.
Now listen to what Paul writes in Romans 6:3–4.
He describes believers being baptized into Christ Jesus and into His death, buried with Him through baptism, so that they might walk in newness of life.
The Greek expression is beautiful:
ἐν καινότητι ζωῆς
en kainotēti zōēs
“In newness of life.”
Not merely a new religious label.
Not merely a family tradition.
A new life.
A life shaped by the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
This is why baptism is so powerful.
It points beyond itself.
It declares the saving work of Another.
The water is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
The ceremony is not the crucified and risen Lord.
Jesus is.
And baptism must never be presented as a substitute for the grace that comes through Christ.
Yet we should also resist the opposite error of treating baptism as meaningless.
The New Testament speaks of baptism with remarkable seriousness.
Acts 22:16 connects baptism with calling upon the Lord's name and the washing away of sins.
Titus 3:5 speaks of God's saving mercy through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, a text many Christians understand baptismally.
And 1 Peter 3:21 contains words that deserve careful attention:
“Baptism ... now saves you.”
That statement should stop anyone from casually dismissing baptism.
But Peter immediately explains that he is not speaking of the removal of physical dirt from the body.
He connects baptism with an appeal to God for a good conscience, or a pledge of a good conscience, depending on how the Greek word eperōtēma is understood, and with the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Christians disagree about precisely how baptism relates to the saving grace described here.
Sacramental traditions emphasize baptism as a divinely appointed means of grace.

Believer's-baptism traditions generally emphasize baptism as the God-commanded expression of faith, inseparable in the apostolic context from conversion but not independently effective apart from Christ.
What both must affirm is that salvation rests upon the saving work of Jesus Christ, not upon human achievement.
And that brings us to the thief on the cross.
A dying man.
No time to rebuild his reputation.
No opportunity to repair every wrong he had committed.
No possibility of descending into a baptismal pool.
He turns to the crucified Jesus and asks to be remembered.
Jesus promises him paradise.
That scene is one of the most breathtaking demonstrations of grace in all of Scripture.
A guilty man.
A dying Savior.
A promise stronger than death.
The thief was not saved because he had performed enough religious duties.
He was saved by Christ.
But we must use this account carefully.
It demonstrates that God is not incapable of saving someone who dies without baptism.
It does not cancel Jesus' command that disciples be baptized.
Grace is not permission to despise obedience.
And obedience is not permission to boast.
The person who trusts Christ should not casually reject baptism.
But neither should we tell a terrified parent that an infant who dies without baptism is automatically condemned.
Scripture does not authorize us to pronounce such a verdict.
The Bible does not give a detailed, universally agreed explanation of the eternal destiny of every infant who dies.
We should entrust such children to the righteous, merciful character of God rather than manufacture certainty where Scripture has not given it.
Consider the tenderness of Jesus toward children.
In Mark 10:13–16, people bring little children to Him.
The disciples try to stop them.
Jesus becomes indignant.
He welcomes the children.
He embraces them.
He blesses them.
What a picture.
The Son of God, who carried the weight of the world's redemption, takes time to hold children in His arms.
Yet notice something important.
The passage records Jesus blessing children.
It does not record Him baptizing them.
Those who support infant baptism see this as evidence of Christ's welcome of children into His kingdom and covenantal care.
Those who practice believer's baptism see it as powerful support for welcoming, blessing, praying for, and teaching children without assuming that baptism must precede personal faith.
Both agree that children matter deeply to Jesus.
And surely we can agree on this:
No Christian parent should ever be made to feel that loving Jesus means loving their child less.
Whether parents baptize an infant or dedicate that child while awaiting a personal profession of faith, their responsibility does not end at the ceremony.
A child needs more than a religious photograph.
More than a certificate.
More than an annual celebration of something that happened before memory began.
A child needs to hear the Gospel.
To see repentance modeled at home.
To watch parents apologize when they sin.
To learn that prayer is not a performance.
To discover that Scripture is not merely quoted during arguments but obeyed in ordinary life.
A child needs to know that Jesus Christ is not simply the family religion.
He is the living Lord.
And no outward ceremony can replace a heart transformed by the Holy Spirit.
Imagine a man who was baptized as an infant.
He grows up.
He attends church occasionally.
He knows the language of Christianity.
He can recite familiar prayers.
But he has never seriously considered his sin before God.
Never personally trusted Christ.
Never understood the cross beyond a religious symbol.
Then one night, everything changes.
Perhaps his marriage is collapsing.
Perhaps he has been exposed in a secret sin.
Perhaps the success he spent decades chasing has left him spiritually empty.
He opens the Bible.
And for the first time, the Gospel confronts him.
Not as a childhood memory.
As the truth.
He realizes that Jesus did not die merely to make him respectable.
Jesus died for sinners.
For the proud.
For the dishonest.
For the sexually immoral.
For the religious hypocrite.
For the person who smiles in church while hiding a heart full of rebellion.
For people like him.
And for people like us.
He falls to his knees.
“Lord Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Now what should happen?
Here the difference between the two baptismal positions becomes intensely practical.

A Christian who holds to believer's baptism will generally say that this man should now be baptized upon his personal profession of faith, because his infant baptism did not fulfill what that tradition understands Christian baptism to require.

A Christian in a tradition that recognizes infant baptism as valid will generally say that he should not be baptized again, because baptism is received once. Instead, he should repent, believe, and live out the grace and obligations of the baptism he already received.
These are not small differences.
They reflect distinct understandings of the nature of the church, the covenant, and the sacrament or ordinance of baptism.
But listen carefully.
Neither side should tell this man that his deepest need is merely to win the baptism argument.
His deepest need is Jesus Christ.
And whatever baptismal conclusion we reach must be governed by the Gospel.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of works, so that no one may boast.
The Greek word for grace is:
χάρις
charis — “grace,” “favor,” or “gift.”
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward sinners, grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
At the cross, justice was not ignored.
Christ bore sin.
At the resurrection, death did not have the final word.
Christ conquered it.
And through Him, sinners are called to repent, believe, and receive forgiveness.
This is the center of Christian salvation.
Not our denomination.
Not our baptismal certificate.
Not the religious reputation of our parents.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where the question becomes uncomfortable for every one of us.
You can defend believer's baptism and still live in unbelief.
You can defend infant baptism and still neglect the Gospel.
You can understand Greek grammar, quote church history, explain covenant theology, and win theological debates while refusing to surrender the sin you secretly love.
Knowledge of baptism is not the same as knowing Christ.
And being correct about a doctrine does not make spiritual pride acceptable.
Some of us have become experts at arguing about water while avoiding the fire of repentance.
We can explain how baptism should happen.
But cannot explain why we refuse to forgive someone.
We can defend the proper candidate for baptism.
But cannot surrender our bitterness.
We can identify another church's theological weakness.
But cannot admit our own hypocrisy.
What would happen if we brought the same seriousness to our hidden sins that we bring to our public doctrinal disagreements?
What would happen if parents became more concerned about their children's daily encounter with the Gospel than about winning arguments over a baptismal ceremony?
What would happen if pastors taught the whole counsel of God without caricaturing sincere Christians who interpret certain passages differently?
Perhaps our conversations would change.
Perhaps our churches would become places where truth and humility could stand together.
Perhaps more people would finally understand that biblical conviction does not require cruelty.
So, after examining the passages, where does the evidence lead?
My conclusion is that baptism following personal faith has the clearer and more directly demonstrated pattern in the New Testament narratives.
Again and again, the book of Acts presents the proclamation of Christ, a response to the Gospel, and baptism.
The Great Commission connects baptism to making disciples.
Romans 6 connects baptism with union with Christ in His death and resurrection.
Colossians 2 speaks of being raised with Christ through faith.
And the New Testament never explicitly records an infant receiving baptism or gives a direct command to baptize infants.
For these reasons, I believe the strongest straightforward reading of the New Testament supports baptizing those who personally profess faith in Jesus Christ.
But that conclusion must be stated with theological honesty.

The arguments for infant baptism are not simply inventions without biblical reasoning. They arise from broader covenantal and sacramental interpretations that have been defended by serious Christian theologians for centuries.
A Christian can disagree with those interpretations without denying the sincerity or Christian identity of everyone who holds them.
And a Christian who was baptized as an infant should not be told that God has never worked in their life merely because another believer questions the timing of their baptism.
The central question is not whether your parents loved you enough to arrange a ceremony.
It is whether you are trusting the living Christ today.

If you were baptized as an infant, ask yourself whether you have personally repented and believed the Gospel. Study the Scriptures carefully, speak with faithful Christian leaders, and seek to obey Christ according to a well-formed biblical conscience.
If you have believed in Christ but have never been baptized, do not treat His command as unimportant. Seek baptism in a faithful local church.
If you were baptized after professing faith, do not use that experience as a reason to look down on Christians from other traditions.
And if you are a parent holding a newborn child, remember that your most enduring spiritual responsibility is not fulfilled in one moment at the front of a church.
You have years of discipleship ahead.
Years of prayers.
Years of Scripture.
Years of hard conversations.
Years of demonstrating what it means to repent when you are wrong.
Years of reminding your child that the Gospel is good news for sinners, not a trophy for perfect families.
You cannot repent on behalf of your child.
You cannot manufacture saving faith in their heart.
But you can proclaim Christ.
You can pray.
You can teach.
You can love.
You can demonstrate the beauty of obedience.
And you can entrust the results to the God who alone gives spiritual life.
There is another reason this conversation matters.
Somewhere right now, a person is reading these words with an old wound.
Maybe they grew up in a church where baptism was treated almost like a guarantee of salvation.
They were told they were spiritually secure, but no one ever explained repentance or personal trust in Christ.
Or perhaps they grew up in a church where people spoke so harshly about infant baptism that they began to question whether their godly parents or grandparents were even genuine Christians.
Maybe their family has been divided over this subject.
Maybe a baptism became an argument at the dinner table.
Maybe a parent and adult child stopped speaking because one changed denominations.
If that is your story, please hear this.
The Gospel does not ask you to abandon truth for the sake of peace.
But it does forbid you to turn truth into a weapon of pride.
Jesus prayed for the unity of His people.
The apostles commanded believers to speak truth in love.
And the same Lord who commands baptism also commands His followers to love one another.
There are genuine doctrinal boundaries.
There are convictions worth defending.
But there is no biblical permission to despise another person simply because a serious theological disagreement exists.
If you believe someone is mistaken, open the Scriptures with them.
Listen.
Explain.
Pray.
And remember that you, too, depend entirely upon grace.
Now I want to ask you something more personal than which church you attend.
If every religious label were removed from your life tonight, what evidence would remain that you belong to Jesus Christ?
Would there be repentance?
Would there be faith?
Would there be a growing desire to obey Him?
Would there be love for His Word?
Would there be the fruit of His Spirit, however imperfectly expressed?
Or would there only be memories of ceremonies, family expectations, and religious traditions?
Do not misunderstand.
Christians are not saved by producing a perfect spiritual record.
The believer's assurance rests upon Jesus Christ and His promises, not flawless performance.
But genuine faith is not indifferent to the Lord it professes to trust.
Jesus calls sinners to follow Him.
Not merely to admire Him.
Not merely to debate Him.
Not merely to use His name in religious arguments.
To follow Him.
Perhaps that is the most important question in this entire discussion.
Not simply, “When should someone be baptized?”
But, “Have I truly come to Christ?”
Because there will come a day when your church membership, religious vocabulary, and family heritage cannot serve as substitutes for the Savior.
On that day, your hope must rest in the crucified and risen Son of God.
And today, while you can still hear His Word, the Gospel invitation remains.
Turn from sin.
Trust Jesus Christ.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Him in obedience.
If you have been hiding behind religion while resisting repentance, you do not need another excuse.
You need the Savior.
And He is not beyond the reach of the broken, ashamed, or guilty person who comes to Him.
John 6:37 records Jesus' promise that the one who comes to Him will certainly not be cast out.
Think about that.
The One who knows every sin you have committed is the One who invites you to come.
Not because sin is harmless.
But because His grace is sufficient to rescue sinners.
That is why our message has always been:
The scandal of our sin is real.
The judgment our sin deserves is real.
The cross is real.
The resurrection is real.
And the mercy offered through Jesus Christ is real.
This is not a story about water having magical power.
It is the story of a Savior who gave His life to redeem sinners and calls His people to respond in faith and obedience.
So whether your baptism happened in a church sanctuary as an infant, in a river after conversion, or has not yet happened at all, do not miss the Person to whom Christian baptism points.
Jesus Christ.
The Lamb of God.
The risen Lord.
The only Savior.
And if this article has challenged something you have always believed, do not immediately become defensive.
Open your Bible.
Read Matthew 28.
Read Acts 2, Acts 8, Acts 10, and Acts 16.
Read Romans 6, Colossians 2, and 1 Peter 3.
Consider the arguments carefully.
Ask God for wisdom.
And let Scripture shape your convictions more deeply than habit, fear, or denominational loyalty.
I also want to invite you into this conversation.
Not into a comment section full of insults.
Into an honest discussion among people who care about the Word of God.
Were you baptized as an infant, after personally believing in Jesus, or have you not yet been baptized? And what passage of Scripture most strongly shapes your understanding?
You can disagree respectfully.
You can tell your testimony.
You can explain how the Lord has been leading you to study this subject.
And if this discussion has revealed that you have been trusting religious activity more than Christ, you can simply comment, “Jesus, teach me to follow You.”
You do not have to reveal anything private to strangers. But perhaps your honest response will help another person realize they are not alone in their questions.
And please do not allow this conversation to end with you.
Not to provoke a fight.
But to encourage a deeper return to Scripture.
There is something else I want to share with you.
Our desire is to help people open the Scriptures, confront difficult questions, understand the Gospel, and grow into deeper obedience to Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers study, pray, mature, and remain grounded in biblical truth.
But I want to be clear about something important.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver.
Your faithfulness to Jesus cannot be measured by a monthly payment.

It can help support the ongoing production of biblical articles, devotional content, and resources for people who might never walk into a church building but may encounter the Gospel through something shared on their phone.
These products are not the reason to give.
The mission is.
One thoughtful comment may encourage a believer to study rather than argue.
One personal invitation may bring a spiritually exhausted friend back into a conversation about Jesus.
We cannot promise what God will do through any particular post.
But we can be faithful with the opportunities before us.
And if this ministry continues to point people to Scripture, repentance, grace, and the saving work of Christ, then every act of prayerful support is part of a mission worth pursuing.
Because in the end, the greatest victory is not that everyone agrees with us about baptism.
The greatest victory is that sinners hear the Gospel, turn to Jesus Christ, and learn to follow Him faithfully.
One day, the debates will be over.
The arguments will fall silent.
The church buildings we know will no longer define our earthly lives.
And all who belong to Christ will see the Savior whose death and resurrection Christian baptism proclaims.
Until then, let us hold firmly to Scripture.
Let us pursue truth with humility.
Let us baptize according to biblical conviction.
Let us teach our children the Gospel.
Let us love the church.
And above everything, let us proclaim Jesus Christ.
Because the most heartbreaking possibility is not that you misunderstood a baptismal tradition.
It is that you spent your whole life defending a sign of belonging to Jesus while never truly coming to the Savior Himself.
